name: Yeshivish Lifecycle, Marriage, and Mourning Glossary Expansion

entries.yeshivish_example: The milah is scheduled for this morning.
entries.plain_english_example: The circumcision ceremony is scheduled for this morning.
meanings: the circumcision component of the covenant ceremony
entries.context_note: Often appears as part of the phrase bris milah. The base glossary already contains bris as the broader ceremony.

entries.yeshivish_example: The mohel will arrive before the bris.
entries.plain_english_example: The person trained to perform the ritual circumcision will arrive before the ceremony.
entries.context_note: A mohel is the person who performs a Jewish ritual circumcision.

entries.yeshivish_example: His grandfather will be the sandek.
entries.plain_english_example: His grandfather will hold the baby in the honored role during the circumcision.
meanings: honored person who holds the baby during the bris
entries.context_note: A major honor at a bris, traditionally associated with holding the baby during the circumcision.

entries.yeshivish_example: They asked him to be the kvatter at the bris.
entries.plain_english_example: They asked him to help carry the baby into the circumcision ceremony.
meanings: person participating in carrying the baby into the bris
entries.context_note: A Yiddish term for a person given the honor of conveying the baby into the bris ceremony; details of the role vary by custom.

entries.yeshivish_example: She was honored as the kvatterin.
entries.plain_english_example: She was honored to participate in bringing the baby into the circumcision ceremony.
meanings: woman participating in carrying the baby into the bris
entries.context_note: The feminine Yiddish form corresponding to kvatter; exact ceremonial roles vary by community.

entries.yeshivish_example: We are going to the shalom zachar Friday night.
entries.plain_english_example: We are going to the traditional gathering held on the first Friday night after a baby boy is born.
meanings: Friday-night gathering after the birth of a baby boy
entries.context_note: An Ashkenazi custom held on the first Friday night after the birth of a boy.

entries.yeshivish_example: The children came to say Shema at the vach nacht.
entries.plain_english_example: The children came for the traditional gathering on the night before the circumcision.
entries.context_note: A custom observed in some Ashkenazi communities on the night before a bris; practices vary by community.

entries.yeshivish_example: The baby was brought near the kisei shel Eliyahu.
entries.plain_english_example: The baby was brought near the special chair associated with Elijah at the circumcision ceremony.
meanings: chair of Elijah used at a bris
entries.context_note: A special chair associated with Eliyahu Hanavi at a bris.

entries.yeshivish_example: They invited us to the seudas bris.
entries.plain_english_example: They invited us to the festive meal following the circumcision.
entries.context_note: The celebratory meal associated with a bris.

entries.yeshivish_example: The pidyon haben is next week.
entries.plain_english_example: The redemption ceremony for the firstborn son is next week.
entries.context_note: A mitzvah performed for a qualifying firstborn son, in which the father redeems him from a kohen.

entries.yeshivish_example: He is the bechor in the family.
entries.plain_english_example: He is the firstborn son in the family.
entries.context_note: The halachic category of firstborn has specific definitions; in ordinary conversation the word commonly means firstborn.

entries.yeshivish_example: Pidyon haben applies only when the child meets the rules of peter rechem.
entries.plain_english_example: The redemption applies only when the child qualifies as the first issue of the womb under Jewish law.
meanings: halachic firstborn status relevant to pidyon haben
entries.context_note: A technical halachic term used in determining eligibility for pidyon haben.

entries.yeshivish_example: They brought five selaim to the kohen for the pidyon haben.
entries.plain_english_example: They brought the redemption payment to a man of priestly lineage for the firstborn ceremony.
meanings: priest, especially a descendant of Aaron
entries.context_note: A kohen has special roles and restrictions in Jewish law. In this lifecycle section the term is especially relevant to pidyon haben and mourning laws.

entries.yeshivish_example: The father gave the kohen chamisha selaim.
entries.plain_english_example: The father gave the kohen the prescribed five-sela redemption value.
meanings: five selaim used for pidyon haben
entries.context_note: The Torah-prescribed redemption amount for pidyon haben; practical valuation of the silver is a halachic matter.

entries.yeshivish_example: They are making a simchas bas on Sunday.
entries.plain_english_example: They are holding a celebration for the birth and naming of their daughter on Sunday.
entries.context_note: A general term used for a celebration connected with the birth or naming of a girl; customs vary.

entries.yeshivish_example: The krias shem will be during the Torah reading.
entries.plain_english_example: The baby will be formally given her Jewish name during the Torah reading.
meanings: giving or announcing a Jewish name
entries.context_note: Literally calling a name; used for formally giving or announcing a Jewish name.

entries.yeshivish_example: His upsherin will be on his third birthday.
entries.plain_english_example: His traditional first haircut celebration will be on his third birthday.
meanings: traditional first haircut ceremony for a young boy
entries.context_note: A custom in many communities, commonly held around a boy’s third birthday. The Hebrew/Sephardic term chalakah is included as a variant.

entries.yeshivish_example: They left his peyos at the upsherin.
entries.plain_english_example: They left the side-lock areas of his hair uncut at the first haircut ceremony.
meanings: hair at the sides of the head governed by the prohibition against rounding the corners
entries.context_note: Commonly discussed at an upsherin and in everyday Orthodox dress and grooming.

entries.yeshivish_example: She does shadchanus for several families.
entries.plain_english_example: She works at suggesting and facilitating marriage matches for several families.
entries.context_note: The activity or field of matchmaking.

entries.yeshivish_example: They paid the shadchanus gelt after the engagement.
entries.plain_english_example: They paid the customary matchmaking fee after the engagement.
entries.context_note: A Yeshivish/Yiddish expression for payment made to a matchmaker.

entries.yeshivish_example: Who redt this shidduch?
entries.plain_english_example: Who suggested or arranged this marriage match?
meanings: suggest or propose a marriage match
act as the person who brings a shidduch idea
entries.context_note: A Yiddish-derived phrase used in Yeshivish English. Spelling and conjugation vary widely.

entries.yeshivish_example: They met at a beshow before the families continued the shidduch.
entries.plain_english_example: They met at a formal arranged meeting used in some communities before proceeding with the match.
meanings: formal prospective-marriage meeting in some Hasidic communities
entries.context_note: A community-specific shidduch term, especially in some Hasidic circles; not universal Yeshivish usage.

entries.yeshivish_example: The families signed the tenoyim before the wedding.
entries.plain_english_example: The families formalized the engagement arrangements before the wedding.
meanings: ceremony or document associated with an engagement
entries.context_note: Historically a formal set of marriage conditions; in contemporary communities it may refer to an engagement ceremony or document, with practices varying.

entries.yeshivish_example: They made a kinyan when the agreement was finalized.
entries.plain_english_example: They performed a formal Jewish-law act of acquisition to give legal effect to the agreement.
meanings: legal mechanism for creating an obligation or transfer
entries.context_note: A broad halachic concept used in many legal contexts, including marriage-related documents and agreements.

entries.yeshivish_example: They are expecting a baby, so we wished them b'shaah tovah.
entries.plain_english_example: They are expecting a baby, so we wished that everything happen at the proper and favorable time.
meanings: a traditional wish used before a future happy event
entries.context_note: Often used for pregnancy and other anticipated milestones where speakers may avoid congratulating before the event occurs. Usage varies by community.

entries.yeshivish_example: Besoroes tovos; keep us posted.
entries.plain_english_example: May we hear good news; keep us posted.
entries.context_note: A common wish when awaiting an outcome, recovery, birth, match, or other hoped-for development.

entries.yeshivish_example: His aufruf is this Shabbos.
entries.plain_english_example: He will be called to the Torah in the traditional pre-wedding celebration this Sabbath.
meanings: pre-wedding Torah aliyah for a groom
entries.context_note: An Ashkenazi custom in which the groom is called to the Torah, commonly on the Shabbos before the wedding.

entries.yeshivish_example: Her friends are coming for the Shabbos kallah.
entries.plain_english_example: Her friends are gathering with the bride on the Sabbath before the wedding.
meanings: pre-wedding Sabbath gathering for a bride
entries.context_note: A pre-wedding custom whose form varies by community.

entries.yeshivish_example: The kabbalas panim starts an hour before the chuppah.
entries.plain_english_example: The pre-wedding reception begins an hour before the wedding canopy ceremony.
entries.context_note: At an Orthodox wedding, often refers to the separate pre-chuppah receptions for the groom and bride.

entries.yeshivish_example: The witnesses signed documents at the chosson tish.
entries.plain_english_example: The witnesses handled pre-wedding formalities at the groom’s table gathering.
entries.context_note: A Yiddish/Hebrew hybrid term for the groom’s pre-wedding gathering; customs and formalities vary.

entries.yeshivish_example: Everyone gathered for the badeken before the chuppah.
entries.plain_english_example: Everyone gathered for the ceremony in which the groom veils the bride before the wedding canopy.
entries.context_note: A Yiddish term meaning covering or veiling, used for the traditional ceremony before the chuppah.

entries.yeshivish_example: The chuppah is called for six o’clock.
entries.plain_english_example: The wedding-canopy ceremony is scheduled for six o’clock.
meanings: marriage ceremony held beneath the canopy
entries.context_note: Can refer to the physical canopy or, conversationally, to the central wedding ceremony.

entries.yeshivish_example: The rav will be the mesader kiddushin.
entries.plain_english_example: The rabbi will officiate and oversee the Jewish marriage ceremony.
meanings: rabbi or authority who officiates at kiddushin
person arranging the halachic marriage ceremony
entries.context_note: The officiating rabbinic role responsible for properly arranging the marriage ceremony.

entries.yeshivish_example: The ring is given as part of the kiddushin.
entries.plain_english_example: The ring is given as part of the halachic betrothal stage of marriage.
meanings: first legal stage of Jewish marriage
entries.context_note: In the contemporary wedding ceremony, kiddushin and nisuin are performed together even though they are conceptually distinct stages.

entries.yeshivish_example: The first bracha is connected with erusin.
entries.plain_english_example: The first marriage blessing relates to the betrothal stage.
meanings: legal engagement stage, often equivalent to kiddushin in halachic usage
entries.context_note: In classical halachic terminology, erusin is the betrothal stage; it is not identical to a modern social engagement.

entries.yeshivish_example: The chuppah completes the nisuin stage.
entries.plain_english_example: The wedding canopy completes the full-marriage stage of the ceremony.
meanings: completion of the marriage stage following kiddushin
entries.context_note: The second legal stage of Jewish marriage, following kiddushin/erusin.

entries.yeshivish_example: The mesader kiddushin recited birkas erusin over the wine.
entries.plain_english_example: The officiant recited the blessing associated with the betrothal stage over wine.
entries.context_note: The blessing recited at the beginning of the halachic marriage ceremony.

entries.yeshivish_example: The eidim signed the kesubah before the chuppah.
entries.plain_english_example: The witnesses signed the Jewish marriage contract before the ceremony.
entries.context_note: A formal Aramaic marriage document setting out the husband’s obligations and the financial protections due to the wife.

entries.yeshivish_example: He was asked to serve as an eid for the kiddushin.
entries.plain_english_example: He was asked to serve as a halachic witness to the marriage.
entries.context_note: Singular of eidim. Jewish-law witness qualifications depend on the legal context.

entries.yeshivish_example: The eidim watched the ring being given.
entries.plain_english_example: The witnesses observed the act that effects the marriage.
entries.context_note: Plural of eid; marriage requires properly qualified witnesses.

entries.yeshivish_example: He said harei at mekudeshes li when giving the ring.
entries.plain_english_example: He recited the traditional declaration of betrothal while giving the ring.
meanings: you are hereby betrothed to me
opening words of the traditional kiddushin declaration
entries.context_note: A recognizable portion of the formula used when effecting kiddushin. This glossary entry identifies the phrase rather than providing legal instructions.

entries.yeshivish_example: The chosson and kallah went to yichud after the chuppah.
entries.plain_english_example: The bride and groom went to a private room together after the wedding ceremony.
meanings: private time of the bride and groom following the ceremony
entries.context_note: At Ashkenazi Orthodox weddings, commonly refers to the private room entered by the newly married couple after the chuppah.

entries.yeshivish_example: We are invited to sheva brachos tonight.
entries.plain_english_example: We are invited to a newlywed celebration at which the seven marriage blessings may be recited.
meanings: post-wedding meal or celebration during the first week
entries.context_note: Can mean the seven blessings themselves or a meal during the post-wedding week at which they are recited when the requirements are met.

entries.yeshivish_example: They are still in the sheva yemei hamishteh.
entries.plain_english_example: They are still within the seven-day wedding celebration period.
entries.context_note: The seven-day celebratory period beginning with the wedding; practical laws depend on circumstances.

entries.yeshivish_example: Do we have panim chadashos for sheva brachos tonight?
entries.plain_english_example: Is there a qualifying new guest for tonight’s seven-blessings meal?
meanings: qualifying new participant for certain sheva-brachos meals
entries.context_note: A technical condition relevant to reciting sheva brachos at meals during the wedding week; details vary by halachic circumstance.

entries.yeshivish_example: They are observing the taanis chosson v'kallah until the chuppah.
entries.plain_english_example: The bride and groom are observing the traditional wedding-day fast until the ceremony.
meanings: wedding-day fast of bride and groom
entries.context_note: A custom in many Ashkenazi communities; exceptions and practices vary.

entries.yeshivish_example: Shviras hakos comes at the end of the chuppah.
entries.plain_english_example: Breaking the glass comes near the end of the wedding ceremony.
meanings: breaking the glass at a Jewish wedding
entries.context_note: A customary act at the conclusion of the chuppah, commonly associated with remembrance of the destruction of Jerusalem.

entries.yeshivish_example: The broken glass is done as a zecher l'churban.
entries.plain_english_example: The broken glass is done as a remembrance of the destruction of the Temple.
meanings: practice commemorating the destruction of Jerusalem and the Temple
entries.context_note: A broad phrase used for customs that preserve remembrance of the Churban, including wedding practices.

entries.yeshivish_example: The mitzvah tantz was held late at the wedding.
entries.plain_english_example: The traditional ceremonial dance was held late in the wedding celebration.
meanings: ceremonial wedding dance in some Hasidic communities
entries.context_note: A Hasidic wedding custom and not universal across Yeshivish or Orthodox communities.

entries.yeshivish_example: The badchan introduced the honors with rhyming verses.
entries.plain_english_example: The traditional wedding entertainer or master of ceremonies introduced the honors with rhyming verses.
entries.context_note: Especially associated with traditional or Hasidic weddings; exact role varies.

entries.yeshivish_example: Everyone sang siman tov u'mazel tov after the chuppah.
entries.plain_english_example: Everyone sang a traditional wish for a good sign and congratulations after the wedding ceremony.
meanings: a good sign and good fortune
traditional celebratory wedding or lifecycle refrain
entries.context_note: A standard celebratory phrase and song used at weddings and other happy lifecycle events. The base glossary separately contains mazel tov.

entries.yeshivish_example: The band started od yishama as the dancing began.
entries.plain_english_example: The band began the traditional wedding song based on the verse about voices of joy being heard again.
meanings: opening words of a traditional Jewish wedding verse and song
entries.context_note: A common shorthand for the wedding verse/song beginning with the words “od yishama.”

entries.yeshivish_example: We wished them a bayis ne'eman b'Yisrael.
entries.plain_english_example: We wished them a faithful and enduring Jewish home.
meanings: traditional blessing for a newly married couple
entries.context_note: A common wedding blessing expressing hope that the couple build a stable Jewish home.

entries.yeshivish_example: May their marriage be a binyan adei ad.
entries.plain_english_example: May their marriage be an enduring union.
entries.context_note: A poetic wedding blessing comparing marriage to an enduring structure.

entries.yeshivish_example: They are still in shana rishona.
entries.plain_english_example: They are still in their first year of marriage.
entries.context_note: In Yeshivish conversation, often specifically refers to a couple’s first year of marriage.

entries.yeshivish_example: They are working on shalom bayis.
entries.plain_english_example: They are working on peace and harmony in their marriage and home.
entries.context_note: Often used specifically for healthy relations between spouses, though literally it means peace in the household.

entries.yeshivish_example: Her baal is learning in the next room.
entries.plain_english_example: Her husband is studying in the next room.
meanings: owner or master in other contexts
entries.context_note: In Yeshivish usage baal can mean husband, but the Hebrew word has several other meanings and requires context.

entries.yeshivish_example: The sugya discusses the status of an eishes ish.
entries.plain_english_example: The Talmudic discussion addresses the status of a married woman.
meanings: woman legally married under Jewish law
entries.context_note: A halachic status term, not merely a conversational synonym for wife.

entries.yeshivish_example: The beis din handles matters of gerushin.
entries.plain_english_example: The rabbinical court handles matters of Jewish divorce.
entries.context_note: The general Hebrew term for divorce, especially in halachic discussion.

entries.yeshivish_example: She received the get through the beis din.
entries.plain_english_example: She received the Jewish bill of divorce through the rabbinical court.
entries.context_note: A properly written and delivered get is central to Jewish divorce law. This glossary entry is descriptive, not procedural.

entries.yeshivish_example: They went to a rav who is experienced as a mesader get.
entries.plain_english_example: They went to a rabbi experienced in arranging a Jewish divorce.
meanings: rabbinic authority who arranges a get
entries.context_note: A specialized role requiring expertise in Jewish divorce law.

entries.yeshivish_example: The matter was brought to a beis din.
entries.plain_english_example: The matter was brought before a rabbinical court.
entries.context_note: A court of dayanim that adjudicates matters under Jewish law; scope and authority depend on context.

entries.yeshivish_example: A dayan reviewed the documents.
entries.plain_english_example: A rabbinical judge reviewed the documents.
entries.context_note: A rabbinic judge qualified to decide matters of Jewish law.

entries.yeshivish_example: The organization helps an agunah obtain a get.
entries.plain_english_example: The organization helps a woman unable to obtain the Jewish divorce needed to remarry under Jewish law.
meanings: woman unable to remarry because her Jewish marriage remains unresolved
entries.context_note: A sensitive halachic and social status. The exact legal situation can arise for more than one reason.

entries.yeshivish_example: The case also involved the status of an agun.
entries.plain_english_example: The case also involved a man whose marital status was halachically unresolved.
meanings: man whose marital status is unresolved or who cannot remarry in a relevant halachic circumstance
entries.context_note: The masculine counterpart term is less common in everyday English than agunah.

entries.yeshivish_example: The beis din issued instructions concerning a mesarev get.
entries.plain_english_example: The rabbinical court addressed a person refusing to cooperate with giving or receiving a required Jewish divorce.
entries.context_note: A sensitive legal label whose proper application depends on the specific beis-din ruling and circumstances.

entries.yeshivish_example: The rav said that a heter meah rabbanim is an exceptional procedure.
entries.plain_english_example: The rabbi said that permission involving one hundred rabbis is an exceptional Jewish-law procedure.
meanings: special dispensation involving one hundred rabbis
entries.context_note: A rare and technical Ashkenazi halachic mechanism with significant procedural requirements.

entries.yeshivish_example: The masechta discusses yibum and chalitzah.
entries.plain_english_example: The tractate discusses levirate marriage and the ceremony that releases the parties from it.
meanings: marriage of a childless widow to her deceased husband’s brother under Torah law
entries.context_note: A technical Torah-law institution whose modern practical treatment depends on community and halachic tradition.

entries.yeshivish_example: They needed a beis din for chalitzah.
entries.plain_english_example: They needed a rabbinical court for the ceremony releasing the widow and brother-in-law from the levirate bond.
meanings: ceremony releasing a widow and brother-in-law from yibum
entries.context_note: A formal halachic ceremony related to yibum.

entries.yeshivish_example: The halacha discusses the obligations of the yavam.
entries.plain_english_example: Jewish law discusses the status of the deceased husband’s brother in a yibum case.
meanings: brother-in-law subject to yibum or chalitzah
entries.context_note: Technical family-law term.

entries.yeshivish_example: The mishnah discusses the yevamah before chalitzah.
entries.plain_english_example: The Mishnah discusses the widow subject to yibum or chalitzah.
meanings: widow subject to yibum or chalitzah
entries.context_note: Technical family-law term.

entries.yeshivish_example: The halacha has specific rules concerning an almana.
entries.plain_english_example: Jewish law has specific rules concerning a widow.
entries.context_note: Common Hebrew/halachic term for a widow.

entries.yeshivish_example: He became an alman several years ago.
entries.plain_english_example: He became a widower several years ago.
entries.context_note: Hebrew term for a widower; less frequent in Yeshivish English than almana.

entries.yeshivish_example: The discussion concerns the status of a gerusha.
entries.plain_english_example: The discussion concerns the status of a divorced woman.
entries.context_note: A legal-status term with particular relevance in some areas of Jewish law.

entries.yeshivish_example: The term mamzer has a very specific halachic meaning.
entries.plain_english_example: The term refers to a narrowly defined Jewish-law lineage status, not simply to an illegitimate child.
meanings: specific prohibited-lineage status under Jewish law
entries.context_note: A sensitive and frequently mistranslated halachic status; it should not be rendered simply as “bastard” or “illegitimate child.”

entries.yeshivish_example: The same lineage rules can apply to a mamzeres.
entries.plain_english_example: The same narrowly defined lineage status can apply to a woman.
meanings: female person with the halachic status of mamzer
entries.context_note: Feminine form of mamzer; a sensitive technical status.

entries.yeshivish_example: We heard about his petirah this morning.
entries.plain_english_example: We heard about his passing this morning.
entries.context_note: A common respectful Hebrew/Yeshivish term for a person’s death.

entries.yeshivish_example: The niftar was well known in the community.
entries.plain_english_example: The deceased man was well known in the community.
entries.context_note: Masculine term commonly used respectfully for the deceased.

entries.yeshivish_example: The nifteres taught for many years.
entries.plain_english_example: The deceased woman taught for many years.
entries.context_note: Feminine counterpart of niftar.

entries.yeshivish_example: The halacha discusses kavod hameis.
entries.plain_english_example: Jewish law discusses the honor due to the deceased.
meanings: corpse or deceased person in halachic terminology
entries.context_note: A direct halachic term that can sound clinical in ordinary English; respectful speech often uses niftar/nifteres instead.

entries.yeshivish_example: The sugya discusses what happens after meisah.
entries.plain_english_example: The Talmudic discussion addresses what happens after death.
entries.context_note: A halachic/textual term for death; not the usual condolence expression.

entries.yeshivish_example: The levaya will leave the shul at noon.
entries.plain_english_example: The funeral procession will leave the synagogue at noon.
meanings: funeral procession or accompanying the deceased
entries.context_note: Literally accompanying; commonly means the funeral or procession accompanying the deceased to burial.

entries.yeshivish_example: Levayas hameis is considered a major chesed.
entries.plain_english_example: Accompanying the deceased to burial is considered an important act of kindness.
entries.context_note: The mitzvah or act of accompanying the deceased, broader than merely attending a funeral service.

entries.yeshivish_example: The kevurah took place that afternoon.
entries.plain_english_example: The burial took place that afternoon.
entries.context_note: The act of burying the deceased.

entries.yeshivish_example: They went to the kever on the yahrzeit.
entries.plain_english_example: They visited the grave on the anniversary of the death.
entries.context_note: Common Hebrew/Yeshivish term for a grave.

entries.yeshivish_example: The levaya continued to the beis hachaim.
entries.plain_english_example: The funeral continued to the Jewish cemetery.
meanings: Jewish cemetery, literally house of life
entries.context_note: A traditional euphemistic name for a cemetery.

entries.yeshivish_example: They purchased a plot in the beis olam.
entries.plain_english_example: They purchased a burial plot in the cemetery.
entries.context_note: Another traditional Hebrew term for a cemetery.

entries.yeshivish_example: The chevra kadisha arranged the taharah and burial.
entries.plain_english_example: The Jewish burial society arranged the ritual preparation and burial.
meanings: group responsible for care of the deceased and burial
entries.context_note: Literally holy society; commonly the organization or volunteers handling traditional Jewish burial preparations.

entries.yeshivish_example: Serving on the chevra kadisha is called a chesed shel emes.
entries.plain_english_example: Caring for the deceased is described as a kindness that cannot be repaid by the recipient.
entries.context_note: Often applied to burial and funeral care because the deceased cannot repay the favor.

entries.yeshivish_example: They changed the schedule because of kavod hameis.
entries.plain_english_example: They changed the schedule to preserve the dignity and honor of the deceased.
meanings: dignity owed to a dead person
entries.context_note: A central principle affecting treatment, transport, burial, and other decisions concerning the deceased.

entries.yeshivish_example: The chevra kadisha performed taharas hameis.
entries.plain_english_example: The burial society performed the traditional ritual preparation and purification of the deceased.
meanings: ritual preparation and purification of the deceased before burial
entries.context_note: This phrase distinguishes burial taharah from family-purity uses of the word taharah.

entries.yeshivish_example: They arranged shmira until the levaya.
entries.plain_english_example: They arranged for the deceased not to be left unattended before the funeral.
meanings: guarding or attending the body before burial
entries.context_note: Traditional practice of maintaining a watch over the deceased until burial.

entries.yeshivish_example: A shomer hameis stayed there overnight.
entries.plain_english_example: A person assigned to watch over the deceased remained there overnight.
meanings: person who watches over the deceased before burial
entries.context_note: The person performing shmira.

entries.yeshivish_example: The niftar was dressed in tachrichim.
entries.plain_english_example: The deceased was dressed in traditional Jewish burial shrouds.
entries.context_note: Traditional Jewish burial garments.

entries.yeshivish_example: The aron was carried to the graveside.
entries.plain_english_example: The coffin was carried to the graveside.
meanings: casket; also means cabinet or ark in other contexts
entries.context_note: In burial context aron means coffin or casket; in synagogue context the same word can mean the Torah ark, so context is essential.

entries.yeshivish_example: The rav discussed whether the delay creates a problem of halanas hameis.
entries.plain_english_example: The rabbi discussed whether delaying the burial overnight raises a Jewish-law concern.
entries.context_note: A technical burial-law concept with exceptions and details that require halachic guidance.

entries.yeshivish_example: The Gemara discusses the special obligations of a meis mitzvah.
entries.plain_english_example: The Talmud discusses the special duty to bury an unattended deceased person.
meanings: deceased person with no one available to arrange burial
entries.context_note: A technical halachic category carrying unusually strong burial obligations.

entries.yeshivish_example: A kohen has to be careful about tumas meis.
entries.plain_english_example: A kohen must be careful about ritual impurity associated with contact or proximity to the dead.
meanings: ritual impurity associated with a corpse
entries.context_note: A technical ritual-purity category especially relevant to kohanim and burial settings.

entries.yeshivish_example: The rosh yeshiva gave a hesped at the levaya.
entries.plain_english_example: The head of the yeshiva delivered a eulogy at the funeral.
meanings: formal words of mourning and praise for the deceased
entries.context_note: A funeral or memorial eulogy, usually focused on the deceased’s life and loss.

entries.yeshivish_example: He was asked to be maspid at the levaya.
entries.plain_english_example: He was asked to deliver a eulogy at the funeral.
entries.context_note: The person who gives a hesped.

entries.yeshivish_example: They recited El Malei Rachamim at the memorial.
entries.plain_english_example: They recited the traditional memorial prayer asking for divine mercy for the deceased.
meanings: Jewish memorial prayer for the deceased
entries.context_note: A memorial prayer commonly recited at funerals, memorial occasions, and cemetery visits in many Ashkenazi communities.

entries.yeshivish_example: During aninus, the immediate family has a distinct halachic status.
entries.plain_english_example: Before burial, immediate mourners have a distinct Jewish-law status with special rules.
meanings: period between death and burial for an immediate mourner
entries.context_note: A technical status applying to specified close relatives before burial; practical rules require halachic guidance.

entries.yeshivish_example: He was an onen until the kevurah.
entries.plain_english_example: He had the special pre-burial status of an immediate mourner until burial.
entries.context_note: Masculine person-form corresponding to aninus.

entries.yeshivish_example: She was an onenes until the burial.
entries.plain_english_example: She had the special pre-burial status of an immediate mourner until burial.
entries.context_note: Feminine person-form corresponding to aninus.

entries.yeshivish_example: He is still in aveilus for a parent.
entries.plain_english_example: He is still observing the Jewish mourning period for a parent.
meanings: halachic state and practices of bereavement
entries.context_note: The general term for Jewish mourning observance after burial.

entries.yeshivish_example: The avel is saying Kaddish.
entries.plain_english_example: The mourner is reciting Kaddish.
entries.context_note: Singular masculine/general form for a mourner.

entries.yeshivish_example: Neighbors brought food for the aveilim.
entries.plain_english_example: Neighbors brought food for the mourners.
entries.context_note: Plural of avel.

entries.yeshivish_example: They are sitting shiva at the family home.
entries.plain_english_example: They are observing the seven-day mourning period at the family home.
entries.context_note: The intensive seven-day mourning period counted from burial, subject to rules concerning holidays and other circumstances.

entries.yeshivish_example: Minyan will be at the beis avel.
entries.plain_english_example: The prayer quorum will meet at the house of mourning.
meanings: home where shiva is being observed
entries.context_note: Often the location where visitors come for nichum aveilim and where prayer services are held during shiva.

entries.yeshivish_example: The family is still within shloshim.
entries.plain_english_example: The family is still within the thirty-day mourning period.
meanings: first thirty days from burial including shiva
entries.context_note: The thirty-day mourning period counted from burial; restrictions differ by relationship to the deceased and other circumstances.

entries.yeshivish_example: For a parent, some aveilus continues through yud beis chodesh.
entries.plain_english_example: For a parent, aspects of mourning continue through the twelve-month period.
meanings: twelve-month mourning period for a parent
entries.context_note: A common Yeshivish shorthand for the extended mourning period for a parent.

entries.yeshivish_example: The aveilim made keriah before the burial.
entries.plain_english_example: The mourners tore a garment as required in the mourning ritual.
entries.context_note: A formal mourning act performed by specified mourners, generally around the funeral or burial depending on custom.

entries.yeshivish_example: We went for nichum aveilim after work.
entries.plain_english_example: We went to comfort the mourners after work.
entries.context_note: The mitzvah of comforting mourners, commonly performed by visiting during shiva.

entries.yeshivish_example: We went to be menachem avel.
entries.plain_english_example: We went to comfort the mourner.
meanings: person or act of consoling a mourner, depending on construction
entries.context_note: Commonly appears in the phrase “to be menachem avel,” meaning to pay a condolence visit.

entries.yeshivish_example: Neighbors prepared the seudas havraah after the kevurah.
entries.plain_english_example: Neighbors prepared the traditional first meal for the mourners after burial.
meanings: first meal provided to mourners after the funeral
entries.context_note: The first meal eaten by mourners after burial, traditionally provided by others.

entries.yeshivish_example: His yahrzeit is next week.
entries.plain_english_example: The annual Jewish-calendar anniversary of his death is next week.
entries.context_note: A Yiddish term for the annual anniversary of a person’s death, observed according to the Jewish calendar.

entries.yeshivish_example: The family marked the yom hashanah with learning and tzedakah.
entries.plain_english_example: The family marked the anniversary of the death with Torah study and charity.
entries.context_note: Literally anniversary; in mourning context it can refer to the yahrzeit.

entries.yeshivish_example: She lit a yahrzeit candle before nightfall.
entries.plain_english_example: She lit a memorial candle for the anniversary of the death.
meanings: memorial candle lit for a yahrzeit
entries.context_note: A candle or light traditionally kindled for a yahrzeit and certain memorial occasions.

entries.yeshivish_example: They lit a ner neshama in his memory.
entries.plain_english_example: They lit a memorial light in memory of the deceased.
entries.context_note: A Hebrew term for a memorial light, often used for yahrzeit or other remembrance.

entries.yeshivish_example: The family visited the matzeivah.
entries.plain_english_example: The family visited the gravestone.
entries.context_note: Commonly means the headstone or monument marking a Jewish grave.

entries.yeshivish_example: The hakamas matzeivah will be after shloshim.
entries.plain_english_example: The dedication or setting of the gravestone will take place after the thirty-day period.
meanings: setting or dedication of a gravestone
entries.context_note: Communities differ on timing and ceremony; sometimes described in English as an unveiling.

entries.yeshivish_example: The shiur was sponsored l'ilui nishmas his father.
entries.plain_english_example: The Torah class was sponsored for the spiritual elevation of his father’s soul.
meanings: for the elevation of the soul of
in memory of, with spiritual merit intended for the deceased
entries.context_note: Common dedication phrase before the name of a deceased person.

entries.yeshivish_example: They learned Mishnayos for an aliyas neshama.
entries.plain_english_example: They studied in the hope of bringing spiritual elevation to the deceased soul.
meanings: spiritual ascent or merit for the deceased
entries.context_note: Used when discussing mitzvos, Torah learning, or charity performed in memory of the deceased.

entries.yeshivish_example: May the neshama have an aliyah.
entries.plain_english_example: May the soul experience spiritual elevation.
entries.context_note: A broad religious term; in mourning conversation it often specifically means the soul of the deceased.

entries.yeshivish_example: Baruch Dayan Ha'emes; we just heard the news.
entries.plain_english_example: Blessed is the true Judge; we just heard the news of the death.
meanings: traditional response or blessing upon hearing of a death
entries.context_note: A traditional Jewish response to news of a death. The exact blessing with God’s name has halachic rules; conversational use often omits the divine-name formula.

entries.term: Hamakom yenachem eschem b'soch sha'ar aveilei Tzion v'Yerushalayim
entries.aleph_beis: המקום ינחם אתכם בתוך שאר אבלי ציון וירושלים
entries.yeshivish_example: Before leaving, he said Hamakom yenachem eschem.
entries.plain_english_example: Before leaving, he recited the traditional Ashkenazi words of comfort to the mourners.
meanings: may God comfort you among the mourners of Zion and Jerusalem
entries.context_note: A standard Ashkenazi condolence formula used during shiva. Gender and singular/plural forms can vary.

entries.yeshivish_example: Rabbi Cohen, zichrono livracha, taught here for decades.
entries.plain_english_example: Rabbi Cohen, of blessed memory, taught here for decades.
meanings: may his memory be a blessing
entries.context_note: A respectful phrase after the name of a deceased man; often abbreviated z”l.

entries.yeshivish_example: Mrs. Cohen, zichrona livracha, founded the program.
entries.plain_english_example: Mrs. Cohen, of blessed memory, founded the program.
meanings: may her memory be a blessing
entries.context_note: Feminine form of zichrono livracha.

entries.yeshivish_example: The sefer quotes Rav Moshe, zecher tzaddik livracha.
entries.plain_english_example: The book quotes Rav Moshe, may the memory of the righteous be a blessing.
meanings: may the memory of the righteous be a blessing
honorific for a deceased righteous person
entries.context_note: A reverential phrase often used after the name of a deceased rabbinic or righteous figure; commonly abbreviated zt”l.

entries.yeshivish_example: His father, alav hashalom, was a longtime gabbai.
entries.plain_english_example: His late father, may he rest in peace, was a longtime synagogue official.
meanings: respectful phrase for a deceased man
entries.context_note: A traditional phrase appended to the name or reference to a deceased man; often abbreviated a”h.

entries.yeshivish_example: Her mother, aleha hashalom, was known for her chesed.
entries.plain_english_example: Her late mother, may she rest in peace, was known for her kindness.
meanings: respectful phrase for a deceased woman
entries.context_note: Feminine counterpart of alav hashalom.

entries.yeshivish_example: His name was followed by Hashem yikom damo.
entries.plain_english_example: His name was followed by the traditional phrase asking God to avenge his blood.
meanings: honorific used for a Jew killed through violence or persecution
entries.context_note: Traditionally used for someone killed because of anti-Jewish violence or persecution; application should follow community convention and context.

entries.yeshivish_example: They mentioned the rebbe, zechuso yagen aleinu.
entries.plain_english_example: They referred to the deceased righteous leader with the phrase “may his merit protect us.”
meanings: reverential phrase for a deceased righteous person
entries.context_note: Common after names of revered deceased rabbis or tzaddikim; frequently abbreviated זיע״א.

entries.yeshivish_example: The inscription ends with tehei nishmaso tzrurah b'tzror hachayim.
entries.plain_english_example: The inscription ends with the traditional wish that his soul be bound in the bond of life.
meanings: may his soul be bound in the bond of life
entries.context_note: A traditional memorial phrase commonly represented on gravestones by the Hebrew abbreviation תנצב״ה; feminine grammar may differ depending on the person.

entries.yeshivish_example: Please accept our tanchumim.
entries.plain_english_example: Please accept our condolences.
entries.context_note: General Hebrew term for condolences or consolation after a loss.

entries.yeshivish_example: Rachmana litzlan, there was a terrible accident.
entries.plain_english_example: May the Merciful One spare us; there was a terrible accident.
meanings: may the Merciful One save us
entries.context_note: An Aramaic expression used when mentioning tragedy, danger, or something deeply undesirable. It is broader than mourning but common in that context.
